newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unions urge Germany to fund Eurofighter, save jobs.
newsitem.headline: Unions urge Germany to fund Eurofighter, save jobs.

text.p: Trade union leaders of the four countries in the Eurofighter consortium said on Wednesday 50,000 jobs could be lost across Europe if Germany did not quickly commit funds to the military programme.
The Bonn government, under pressure to curb public deficits in a race to set up a single European currency, has stalled on approving 23 billion marks for the project.
That has led Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa), the German industrial partner, to say it will stop work if there is no official funding before the parliamentary summer recess.

"The whole aviation and space industry in Europe is at stake," Ingrid Lullmann, chairwoman of the Dasa works council told a news conference at the Paris air show. "Approximately 50,000 jobs are at stake in Europe," she said.

The German government needs to put up one billion marks this year as its part of the multinational programme, she told Reuters. Eurofighter accounted for two percent of the total Germany defence budget she said, citing a figure of one billion marks a year for 16 years.

Some 18,000 jobs are risk in Germany, she said. Dasa may have to put employees on short time working if the government did not decide by the end of July, she said. She envisaged "protest action" in Bonn if there were no decision by then.

Around 15,000 highly-skilled jobs in Britain hang in the balance, John Dears, a union official at British Aerospace Plc said. Some 120 suppliers also depend on the programme and some had already gone bankrupt because of the German delay.

"It's absolutely crucial the German government make a decision very quickly," he said. "If we're not careful, we are in danger of handing over the defence of the skies of Europe to the Americans," he added.

Gabriele Giuffre, a union official at Alenia, the Italian Eurofighter partner, said 15,000 jobs depended on the programme. The project enjoyed political support from the Italian government, despite changes in administration, he said. Some 2000 billion lire had been committed to the programme.
Javier Ramos, a union official at Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (Casa), said Eurofighter could maintain 10,000 Spanish jobs over 10 to 12 years.
Dasa chief executive Manfred Bischoff said on Sunday at the air show he was confident Bonn would approve funds.

"I am extremely confident that the government will find a solution before the summer break. Discussions with the policy-makers are making good headway," Bischoff said at a news conference. However, "if there is no decision in the cabinet in July, we will stop pre-production activities," he said.

Germany's struggle to close a gaping budget deficit and to qualify for European monetary union has raised concerns about funding its purchase of 180 Eurofighter jets. Britain has already agreed to buy 232 of the aircraft with Italy and Spain buying the balance.
